body:
Partners Group is pressing ahead with fresh dealmaking even as its share price struggles, a contrast that throws the Swiss asset manager's twin challenges into sharp relief: keeping capital inside its funds while convincing public-market investors that the earnings engine remains intact.

On the transaction front, the firm acted as co-lead investor alongside L Catterton in a USD 180 million financing round for Scanntech Uruguay Hosting SA, with Bradesco Bank and SPX Equities also participating. The deal remains subject to customary conditions and regulatory approvals. Separately, Partners Group's private-credit platform arranged a unitranche refinancing with super-senior facilities for Germany's DELABO.group, bundling in acquisition, investment and working-capital lines. The size of that credit package was not disclosed.

Those operational wins have done little to lift the stock. The shares changed hands at EUR 639.20 on the previous session, down 1.3%, and have now surrendered 40% of their value since the start of the year. Another reading put the price at EUR 632.20, with the same year-to-date decline of 40%.

Where the real battle is being fought

What matters more than new mandates, however, is how existing clients behave. The stability of inflows — and above all the prevention of uncontrolled withdrawals from the firm's investment vehicles — will shape the coming quarters. Should the products come under sustained liquidity strain, management fees and, by extension, the group's fundamental valuation would feel it immediately.

That pressure has already surfaced. According to Reuters, Partners Group capped redemptions across several evergreen funds back in June. The mood hardened further at Partners Group Private Equity Limited, the listed UK investment company, where holders representing 74.1% of shares voted in favour of the liquidity option. That outcome scuppered a proposed restructuring and set the vehicle on a path to an orderly wind-down. The vote concerns only that managed entity, not Partners Group Holding AG itself.

The firm's flagship evergreen vehicle is now the focal point. At the start of October, Partners Group unveiled plans to split the Global Value SICAV, which carries a net asset value of EUR 6.6 billion, into two sleeves — one targeting long-term capital growth, the other distributing accumulated returns to investors. The overhaul followed a surge in redemption requests and earlier capped payouts.

Rates add a second layer of pressure

Broader market forces have compounded the unease. Hotter-than-expected US inflation data rekindled interest-rate worries across global trading desks. For private-markets managers, that sting lands twice: a persistently high rate environment complicates dealmaking, compresses valuation multiples on unlisted holdings and keeps institutional clients on the sidelines when it comes to fresh commitments.

Against that backdrop, the firm's leadership has been putting its own money to work. Members of management bought roughly CHF 21 million worth of stock in private transactions between 6 and 8 October, according to media reports. Since the beginning of September, purchases by the board and executives have totalled almost CHF 39 million. Such insider buying signals internal conviction, yet it has so far failed to break the wider market's reticence.

A pivot toward yield-heavy credit

Partners Group is simultaneously broadening its menu of alternative return sources. Last week it launched a global multi-sector private-credit income strategy, structured as an open-ended evergreen fund and aimed at institutional investors and wealthy private clients. The programme targets total returns in the high single-digit to low double-digit percentage range, generated predominantly through ongoing interest and credit income.

That build-out runs in parallel with the Global Value SICAV revamp, which is designed to cater to differing investor preferences by separating growth-oriented and income-distributing mandates. If shareholders sign off on the concept and demand for the new credit products picks up, the manager could steady its asset base and regain operational momentum.

A darker scenario hangs on continued caution across the private-markets sector. Should client skepticism persist, other investment vehicles could meet the same fate as Partners Group Private Equity Limited. A defensive stance among large investors not only curbs fresh inflows but also raises the risk that portfolio companies must be liquidated under unfavourable market conditions.

The pending vote on the Global Value SICAV carries outsized sentiment risk. If investors reject the split and instead demand liquidity, management would have to organise further asset sales — a path that would shrink assets under management, erode performance-related income and prolong the downward pressure on the stock.

What chart watchers are eyeing

For the share price, the decision field is clearly marked. As long as the stock holds above its 52-week low of EUR 623.00, a technical stabilisation remains possible; a break below that support would threaten an immediate extension of the decline. The next concrete catalyst is the shareholder ballot on the Global Value SICAV restructuring, which will tell the market whether investors are prepared to back the proposed overhaul — or whether the push for early repayment of further capital continues.
